# New York Landlord-Tenant Dispute Prep

You have a strong starting position if the carpet issue is ordinary wear and tear and you have move-in photos plus a lease clause excluding it. The goal is to organize proof, request a proper itemized explanation, and keep the tone firm but cooperative.

## Evidence Checklist for the Security Deposit Dispute

- **Lease copy** showing the start date, deposit terms, and the clause excluding normal wear and tear
- **Move-in photos** with dates if available, especially the carpet condition when you took possession
- **Move-out photos/videos** showing the unit condition on 2026-02-28
- **Security deposit records**: receipt, bank transfer, canceled check, or ledger
- **Rent payment history** proving you were current at move-out
- **Landlord’s deduction notice** or any refund letter showing the USD 900 carpet charge
- **Move-out communication**: email/text about keys, inspection, or return of possession
- **Cleaning receipts** if you paid for professional cleaning or stain removal
- **Witness statements** from roommates, guests, or movers who saw the carpet condition
- **Any prior repair requests** or complaints about the carpet, if relevant
- **A timeline note** with dates: lease start, deposit paid, move-out date, refund date, and when the deduction was received

## Practical Evidence Organization Plan

| Item | What to Save | Why It Matters |
|---|---|---|
| Lease | Full signed lease PDF or scan | Proves the wear-and-tear exclusion |
| Photos | Original image files, not screenshots only | Helps show condition and timestamps |
| Deposit proof | Receipt, bank record, or canceled check | Confirms amount and payment date |
| Move-out proof | Photos, video, keys returned, email confirmation | Shows you vacated properly |
| Deduction notice | Landlord’s statement and any receipts provided | Tests whether the charge is specific and supported |
| Communications | Texts/emails in one folder | Creates a clean paper trail |
| Timeline | One-page date log | Makes your story easy to follow |

## Draft Letter Requesting an Itemized Explanation

**Subject:** Request for Itemized Security Deposit Deduction Explanation

Dear [Landlord/Property Manager Name],

I am writing about the security deposit deduction of **USD 900** for alleged carpet damage after I moved out on **2026-02-28**.

My lease states that **normal wear and tear is excluded**, and I have move-in photos showing the carpet’s condition when I took possession on **2025-03-01**. To understand this charge, please send me:

- An itemized written explanation of the carpet deduction
- The specific area(s) of damage being claimed
- Copies of any invoices, receipts, or repair estimates
- Photos or inspection notes supporting the deduction
- The calculation showing how the amount of USD 900 was determined

If the charge relates to ordinary wear and tear, I believe it should not be deducted from the deposit. I would appreciate a written response by **[insert date, 7–10 days from sending]** so we can resolve this promptly and professionally.

Thank you for your attention. I look forward to your reply.

Sincerely,
[Your Full Name]
[Former Address]
[Phone Number]
[Email Address]

## Calm Negotiation Strategy

- **Lead with facts, not accusations.** Keep the conversation focused on photos, lease language, and receipts.
- **Ask for proof before arguing the amount.** A reasonable request for itemization often narrows weak claims quickly.
- **Use one clear position:** the landlord must show that the charge was for actual damage beyond normal wear and tear.
- **Offer a practical resolution.** If there is minor damage, propose a reduced amount only if they provide documentation.
- **Keep messages short and polite.** Avoid emotional language or threats in early exchanges.
- **Document every call in writing.** After a phone call, send a short email recap of what was discussed.
- **Set a deadline.** If they do not respond, send a follow-up and preserve the record for formal escalation.
